items.summary: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).
items.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges

items.summary: This paper addresses decentralized estimation and control of heterogeneous multi-agent systems communicating over directed switching topologies. The objective is to satisfy cooperative tasks that require coordination among agents according to a time-invariant task graph. To address the potential mismatch between the communication and task graphs, each agent is equipped with a k-hop Prescribed Performance State Observer (k-hop PPSO) to estimate the states of agents up to k communication hops away using only information exchanged with its 1-hop neighbors. A novel prescribed performance funnel construction is developed to account for the switching communication topology, and a sufficient lower bound on the dwell-time is derived to guarantee the prescribed performance specifications under topology variations. Further analysis shows that, if the desired control objective is achieved with exact knowledge of the required nonlocal states and the resulting closed-loop system is uniformly set-ISS with respect to the state estimation error, then replacing these states with their estimates guarantees convergence to a neighborhood of the desired set. The size of this neighborhood can be made arbitrarily small by appropriately selecting the observer performance bounds. A simulation study demonstrates task satisfaction under directed switching topologies.
items.title: Observer-Based Control for Multi-Agent Systems under Communication-Task Graph Mismatch and Directed Switching Topologies

items.summary: Porous-material adsorption studies require coordinated structure preparation, force-field selection, simulation, validation, and interpretation, making end-to-end automation difficult. We test whether RaspAssistant, a hierarchical multi-agent framework, can carry an adsorption study from force-field preparation through validation and downstream separation analysis. Across twelve multi-agent workflow-reproduction runs spanning four adsorption and separation benchmarks, overall scores ranged from 8.50 to 10.00 on a rubric evaluating workflow correctness, simulation validity, and analysis consistency. In a separate eight-case force-field extraction benchmark, the mean weighted score was 0.967, combining parameter agreement and RASPA readiness. In open-ended studies, the system diagnosed and refined an acetylene force field and, after validating a CO$_2$ force field against MFI experiments, screened 197 pure-silica zeolites that passed automated input checks. These results demonstrate autonomous workflow execution after task specification and input provision: RaspAssistant coordinates, validates, adapts, and documents extended adsorption-simulation workflows while exposing model sensitivity and methodological limitations for expert review.
items.title: RaspAssistant as an Agentic Framework for Automating Adsorption Simulation Research in Porous Materials

items.summary: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
items.title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI

items.summary: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
items.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing

items.summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.
items.title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents

items.summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.
items.title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems

items.summary: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.
items.title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs

items.summary: Despite rapid progress in text-to-motion generation, existing methods are commonly designed for single-shot generation. When users are dissatisfied with specific motion details, they are often forced to regenerate the entire sequence from scratch, which is computationally inefficient and potentially destroys previously established kinematic context. A practical generation system should instead support iterative user feedback and refine only the affected spatio-temporal regions while preserving the remaining motion. Therefore, we introduce a conversational motion generation paradigm that requires the system to coordinate instruction understanding, motion generation, localized editing, and quality assessment. Recent advances in LLM-driven multi-agent systems provide a promising foundation for such role-specialized coordination. To tackle these challenges, a Self-evolving Multi-Agent RefinemenT Framework (SMART) is proposed for conversational motion generation. Within SMART, to preserve semantic consistency, we design a semantic-guided masked motion editing mechanism, which precisely grounds natural language feedback into spatiotemporal motion regions to enable localized refinements without altering unedited regions. To reduce redundant exploration, we propose a memory-based self-evolving strategy that dynamically accumulates motion editing knowledge from interaction history and reuses past successful experience. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SMART effectively supports multi-turn conversational motion generation and enables efficient motion refinement.
items.title: Learn to Modify: Self-evolving Multi-agent Refinement Framework for Conversational Text-to-Motion Generation

items.summary: Beam hopping technology enables LEO satellites to dynamically switch beam coverage positions, providing flexible resource allocation for non-uniformly distributed traffic demands. However, the severe spatial interference coupling among beams makes coordinated scheduling challenging. To address this problem, in this letter, we propose an interference-graph-aided multi-agent reinforcement learning approach that constructs an interference graph to capture beam coupling relationships and injects this structural prior into agent-side representation learning. Each beam agent aggregates information from interference neighbors via graph convolution before estimating local Q-values, which are then decomposed by the standard mixing network. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 34.4\% higher throughput than QMIX with more stable interference management, under non-uniform traffic and co-channel interference settings.
items.title: Interference-Graph-Aided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Beam Hopping LEO Satellite Networks

items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.
items.title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor

items.summary: Agentic system design is increasingly shifting from hand-crafted prompts and workflows toward automated search over agentic programs and interaction structures, with multi-agent systems receiving growing attention. Yet a central question remains unresolved: when does an automatically generated multi-agent structure exhibit a functionally meaningful division of responsibility? We argue that automated multi-agent design should move beyond searching for effective architectures toward identifying which responsibilities are functionally necessary, how they should be allocated, and when they should change. To explore this, we propose Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design (AMOD), which treats organization itself as a first-class design object, explicitly modeling how agent teams are composed, what functional responsibilities the agents assume, how they coordinate, and how collective decisions are made. We formulate AMOD as an execution-driven design loop. For each task, an automated designer instantiates an organization by assigning functional responsibilities and coordination rules to a set of agents. After execution, task outcomes, intermediate artifacts, and interaction traces are examined to identify which responsibilities may be missing, duplicated, or ineffective, and the organization is revised accordingly. We also propose testing discovered responsibilities by removing them, replacing them with generic roles, or changing their assignment under matched resource budgets, with complementary evaluations. AMOD provides a principled foundation for evidence-based and adaptive multi-agent organization design.
items.title: Automated Multi-Agent Organization Design: From Architecture Search to Organizational Learning

items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Version 3.2.0 adds the attack package for the four targets (barrier atlas, bypass search, superstring chain, the audit of a quantum-gravity manuscript, triage and the figure critic), the bridge index of 243 thirteen-crossing knots by transvection representations, and the constructions of the proof that gravity with the form factor of a scale-invariant brane gas has no ultraviolet divergence at any order of perturbation theory for n ≥ 4 (the brane response and its resonant refuter, the power counting, the one-loop tuning, the vacuum energy and the reflection-positivity refuter), each recorded as a CANDIDATE control until refereed. Version 3.3.0 adds the attempts of 21 October 2026 on the Hodge inputs (F2) and (F3') (three results and five construction rounds, all stopped on named walls), the proof that the mirror-fixed clause of the Geometric Selection Conjecture is empty, so that the conjecture is equivalent to a viable vacuum on a component carrying no standard embedding (control gsc-mirror-clause, CANDIDATE), two exact constructions from the TheoPhysEval benchmark, the final passes on Lehmer's totient problem and the brane gas, and a third pass on the knot tables that settles the nonorientable four-genus of 2,093 of the 3,525 open knots with 11 to 13 crossings (control crosscap4d-13, CANDIDATE). Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: A hardening release from the 2026-10-21 full review ( docs/reviews/2026-10-21-full-review.md ): untrusted bundles and archives can no longer read or write outside themselves or exhaust memory, arkiv convert no longer destroys records, and malformed archives, bundles, and JSONL files report a clean error instead of a traceback (for crafted databases, only colliding asset rows are covered so far; see Known issues). No on-disk structure changes; arkiv_format stays "0.2" . Security S1: README contents entries (and schema.yaml , nested README files, and the archive's own README.md ) that are absolute, contain .. or a backslash, or resolve outside the archive are refused, so a crafted archive can no longer import arbitrary .jsonl files, or the text of any host file, from the host. S2: symlinks under media/ (including a symlinked media/ itself) are never followed or imported, so host files cannot land in the database and then in exported bundles. Directory import, the source fingerprint, and pack_bundle now share one walk ( iter_source_files ). S3: tar bundles are read with bounded headers: GNU long-name and pax headers over 1 MiB, or chained deeper than 8, are refused before they are read into memory, and sparse members are refused. A 65 KB archive no longer needs hundreds of MiB, and unpack_bundle is bounded too. S4: a database path containing # , ? , or % (or non-ASCII characters, or spaces) opens the file it names when opened read-only, instead of opening, and creating, a different file. S5: duplicate tar and zip members are refused on unpack, as are tar hard and symbolic links, FIFOs, and devices, so iter_jsonl and convert can no longer disagree about an archive's content. Names that differ only in case or Unicode normalization ( records.jsonl and Records.jsonl ) count as duplicates, since a case-insensitive filesystem (APFS, NTFS) stores them as one file. S6: MCP sql_query aborts after 10 seconds (an infinite recursive CTE no longer hangs the server) and cuts any text or blob cell over 100000 characters. S7: asset rows in a crafted database can no longer overwrite README.md , *.jsonl , or other non-media files on export; only canonical paths under media/ are written, checked on the resolved path. Fixed L1: arkiv convert <dir> after MCP write_record no longer silently deletes the written records; it refuses and names the export command. L2: reconverting a directory into its existing database rebuilds it from scratch, so collections, README text, and schema descriptions removed from the directory are gone from the database too, and status no longer reports in_sync over stale content. L3: records with a wrongly typed known field ( "metadata": null or a list, object or array content , list mimetype , boolean content ) no longer crash the import with a traceback or store "1" . L4: a high-cardinality key's example is stored apart from its enumerated values , so it is no longer written back as a bogus curated values: [id-0] ; a stale values from an earlier export heals on the next convert and export. C1: following the guard's advice ( arkiv convert x.db x ) now clears it; a full db-to-directory export records the directory and resets the unexported-writes counter. C5: a UTF-8 byte order mark no longer drops the first record of a JSONL file, in parse_jsonl , in the bundle readers, and in arkiv detect and arkiv fix (which keeps the mark when it rewrites the file). C6: zip packing no longer fails on a member of 2 GiB or more ( pack_bundle declares each member's size up front so zipfile switches to zip64 for members over 2 GiB), and write_bundle and pack_bundle write atomically, so a failure leaves no partial bundle behind. C7: corrupt, truncated, or encrypted bundles, and files that are not the archive their extension claims (a non-zip named .zip ), report a clean ValueError instead of a traceback ( zlib.error , NotImplementedError , RuntimeError , EOFError , BadZipFile , tarfile.ReadError ), in unpack
items.title: queelius/arkiv: arkiv 0.4.1

items.summary: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.
items.title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong

items.summary: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
items.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model

items.summary: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
items.title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development

items.summary: Differentiable logic-gate networks (DLGNs) are attractive for irrigation controllers because their learned Boolean structure can be verified exhaustively, yet the safety case for deploying them under actuator-failure cascades has not been formalised. The work is a design-and-power analysis of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation protocol, not an observational study: no field data are used or claimed. Operating characteristics were characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point compliance effect at 80% power under this variance structure, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the design's sensitivity. A formal-safety audit of DLGN controllers is then specified as a finite-state reachability problem over the actuator-failure cascade, with water-rights compliance encoded as an invariant. The contribution is a benchmark protocol that couples a verifiable controller class to a statistically defensible evaluation design, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not the controller, is the binding constraint on regulatory acceptance.
tags: differentiable logic-gate networks; irrigation controllers; actuator-failure cascades; water-rights
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Differentiable Logic-Gate Networks for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Controllers Under Actuator-Failure Cascades: An Artificial Intelligence Formal-Safety Audit for Water-Rights Compliance

items.summary: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.
items.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents

items.summary: Generative recommenders replace the retrieve-then-rank cascade with a single model: beam search over semantic item identifiers performs retrieval, and the same likelihood performs ranking. We show that this shared score makes them forget long-tail items twice. In retrieval, beam search keeps identifier prefixes by the probability mass of their subtrees, so tail items are pruned early, and a wider beam admits few more of them. In ranking, the likelihood places tail items below head items even when they are admitted, so expanding retrieval alone brings little or no gain. Both failures reflect missing item-level memorization (i.e., direct recall of which items co-occur), which collaborative filtering provides and shared-prefix generation lacks. To this end, we propose CAPE (Co-occurrence-Aware Pool Expansion), a training-free plug-in that restores memorization at both stages: (i) a memorization channel retrieves co-occurrence-supported tail items outside the beam and scores them with the frozen generator, and (ii) memorization-calibrated ranking fuses the generator likelihood with co-occurrence evidence while keeping the generator's first item. Experiments with two generative backbones on product and music domains show that CAPE significantly improves long-tail accuracy over the backbones and over re-ranking baselines that share its candidates, preserves or improves overall accuracy, and adds a small fraction of the latency.
items.title: Generative Recommenders Forget the Long Tail: Restoring Memorization in Retrieval and Ranking

items.summary: We study inhomogeneous random graphs on $n$ vertices with independent Pareto weights of parameter $α>0$ and connection probabilities $\min(\varepsilon_n W_iW_j, 1)$. Our main focus is the infinite-mean regime $0<α<1$. Under the scaling $n\varepsilon_n^α=λ$, with $λ>0$ fixed, the global architecture of the graph is entirely governed by the Poisson point process $Π$ of rescaled extreme weights. In particular, the size of the largest component, divided by $n$, converges to a non-degenerate random variable expressed as an explicit functional of $Π$. Through the point process $Π$, we also characterize the exact limiting connectivity probability, uncovering a non-sharp connectivity threshold. The second largest component and the diameter of the largest component are bounded with high probability. The distance between two uniformly chosen vertices in the largest component is at most three with high probability. We also prove convergence of the point process of rescaled degrees and identify the limiting distribution of the maximum degree. For completeness, we obtain expected degree asymptotics, typical degree limits and connectivity regimes for all $α>0$. Due to the failure of classical branching process approximations in the infinite-mean regime, our approach relies fundamentally on analyzing the extreme weight environment $Π$.
items.title: Inhomogeneous random graphs: how heavy tails reshape connectivity

items.summary: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
items.title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models

items.summary: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.
items.title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing

The most common reason for this is that the pipeline accesses proprietary data that users are not allowed to access directly, but that may be used as e.g. a reference panel for imputation. items.summary: Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.
items.title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits

items.summary: Background:  Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have revolutionized the therapeutic landscape of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), heart failure (HF), and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Beyond their primary glucose-lowering actions, both drug classes exert profound organ-protective effects. Objective:  This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on the molecular, cellular, and physiological mechanisms driving the cardio- and nephroprotective outcomes of SGLT2i and GLP-1RAs. Methods:  A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases following PRISMA guidelines for studies published between 2018 and 2026. Results:  SGLT2i act primarily via hemodynamic restoration, reducing intraglomerular pressure through tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF), shifting myocardial energetics toward ketone utilization, inhibiting Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger 1 and 3 (NHE1/NHE3), and suppressing renal/cardiac inflammation and fibrosis. GLP-1RAs act predominantly via anti-inflammatory pathways, endothelial protection, reduction of oxidative stress, inhibition of vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, and attenuation of renal hyperfiltration via systemic anti-atherosclerotic pathways. Conclusion: SGLT2i and GLP-1RAs display distinct yet complementary molecular pathways. Their synergistic mechanism provides a strong rationale for combined therapy to achieve optimal cardiorenal protection in clinical practice.
tags: SGLT2 inhibitors; GLP-1 receptor agonists; Cardioprotection; Nephroprotection; Tubuloglomerular feed
items.title: MOLECULAR MECHANISMS UNDERLYING THE CARDIO- AND NEPHROPROTECTIVE EFFECTS OF SGLT2 INHIBITORS AND GLP-1 RECEPTOR AGONISTS: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW

items.summary: Omni-modal assistants must remember not only what users say, but also what they show and convey. Existing long-term memory benchmarks are mostly text-and-image or report a single end-to-end score, so they cannot locate whether evidence is lost when it is represented, retrieved, delivered, or read. We introduce MOSAIC, a benchmark of 923 questions over persona-grounded histories of 11-24 sessions spanning text, image, video, and audio. MOSAIC constructs targeted spatial, temporal, and prosodic signals rather than decorative media, with the strongest causal validation for spatial information and selector-level validation for annotated prosody, and pairs them with a matched diagnostic protocol that freezes the question, reader, prompt, and budget while intervening on representation, retrieval, and delivery. Matched decomposition shows that representation loss is modality-dependent, residual reading dominates even under gold evidence, and abstention remains weak on these controls: strong answerable scores coexist with failures to refuse. MOSAIC thus turns omni-modal memory evaluation from a leaderboard into a diagnosis of write, retrieve, deliver, and read failures.
items.title: MOSAIC: An Omni-Modal Benchmark for Long-Term Memory and Cross-Modal Reasoning in Conversational Agents

items.summary: In this paper, we investigate why vision-language models (VLMs) produce errors by decomposing them into two sources: visual-representation failures, in which the visual evidence required for the correct answer is not encoded, and visual-utilization failures, in which this evidence is encoded but not successfully used. We propose to estimate the visual-utilization failure rate using lightweight probes and derive theoretical bounds on the true rate that account for probe imperfections. We introduce VELens (Visual Evidence Lens), a rank-based probe that traces visual evidence for both a target object and its ground-truth attribute, such as color, material, or shape, across VLM layers. We evaluate VELens on over 6,000 images using LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Our method achieves ROC-AUC scores of 0.95 and 0.91, respectively, and outperforms alternative probes in both low-resource and unseen-attribute settings. Using it to diagnose errors, we estimate that visual-utilization failures account for 84.4% of LLaVA errors and 70.0% of Qwen errors, with conservative lower bounds of 77.5% and 61.0%, respectively. Overall, our study identifies visual utilization as the dominant bottleneck in VLMs and suggests that a central opportunity for improvement lies in developing better mechanisms to locate, route, and use the visual information they already encode.
items.title: Encoded but Unused: Bounding the Sources of VLM Errors

items.summary: Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have seen broad adoption, but their biases are still far less examined than those of standard LLMs, creating possible social harms when deployed in real-world settings. Prior efforts to extend bias analyses from LLMs into the multi-modal space either cover only a few bias categories or do not ensure that the groups being compared are clearly addressed by visual cues in the images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Melange, a wide-ranging synthetic visual benchmark covering seven categories for assessing social biases in MLLMs. It is grounded in the widely used language-only BBQ dataset (Bias Benchmark for Question Answering) from BigBench, carefully extending its constructed contexts via controlled generation of visual scenarios so the target attributes appear visually and clearly. To maximize reliability, our generated images pass through two stages of validation: automated screening using visual question answering (VQA) and subsequent manual inspection by human annotators. By systematically evaluating 23 open-source MLLMs across three matched evaluation settings---text-only, image-only, and image-with-context---Melange isolates the fairness effect of the input modality. Switching from text to vision reduces fairness by 0.291 on average, a gap that varies by model family rather than by scale alone. A perception control confirms that this gap is not an artifact of visual comprehension: models identify the depicted attributes at 90--95\% accuracy yet still fail to abstain. When models do commit to a biased answer, polarity-aware stereotype alignment shows they choose the human-stereotypical response roughly three-quarters of the time.
items.title: Melange: A Synthetic Visual Bias Benchmark for Multi-modal Large Language Models

items.summary: This dataset provides supporting numerical artifacts for the manuscript “Reduced-Regularity Consistency for a Direct ABC-Adapted L1-Type Operator: Analysis and Diffusion Benchmarks.” The archive contains the locked Problem-1 FDM/FEM common-resolution results, the Chebyshev spectral results, the Problem-1 temporal-contamination audit and its derived summary, the Problem-2 Q=64 FDM/Spectral graded-mesh validation results, and the FEM Pilot-2 console-verified summary. A README, artifact manifest, and SHA-256 checksum list document the archive contents, integrity checks, evidence status, and item-specific limitations. This is a supporting-data archive, not a complete source-code or computational-environment release. The archived CSV files were retained from the project artifacts and integrity-checked during packaging; the original numerical experiments were not rerun for this deposit. The FEM Pilot-2 file is a console-verified summary rather than a complete raw export. Known provenance limitations are documented in the accompanying README and manifest. The Q=64 results show refinement trends consistent with the stated consistency upper bound for the tested cases. They do not establish sharpness of the estimate or an unconditional fully discrete convergence theorem.
tags: Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative; fractional diffusion; ABC-L1 discretization; numerical analysis;
items.title: Supporting numerical data for: Reduced-Regularity Consistency for a Direct ABC-Adapted L1-Type Operator: Analysis and Diffusion Benchmarks

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.
items.title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs

items.summary: Yield anomaly detectors in computer agriculture routinely attribute harvest shortfalls to a single dominant stressor, yet drought and pest outbreaks frequently co-occur and confound one another's signatures in remotely sensed and agronomic covariates. The framework is methodological and theoretical: it defines the attribution game, states the confounding conditions under which Shapley values are point-identified, and derives upper and lower bounds when concurrent drought and pest outbreak render the attribution non-identified. A worked illustration uses NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Accra, Ghana (5.6, -0.19) over 2000-2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 26.521 C, a standard deviation of 1.24 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, to show how a single covariate channel can be bounded before attribution is attempted. The contribution is a bound-based audit protocol that replaces point attribution with interval attribution and specifies the evidence required to narrow those intervals in operational detector pipelines.
tags: causal attribution; Shapley decomposition; yield anomaly detection; drought-pest confounding; comput
items.title: Evaluation of Causal-Attribution Bounds for Computer Agriculture Yield Anomaly Detectors Under Concurrent Drought and Pest Outbreak Confounding: An Artificial Intelligence Shapley-Decomposition Audit

items.summary: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
items.title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts

items.summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used as sources of knowledge for large language models (LLMs), hybrid AI systems, autonomous agents, and machine reasoning. However, conventional knowledge representation does not, by itself, establish whether a KG fact is ethically appropriate for a particular use, legitimately accessible to a particular agent, or endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. This paper proposes an EPB-passport framework that associates knowledge claims with explicit qualifications concerning Ethics, Privacy, and Bias (EPB). At the level of an RDF triple, the passport records whether a claim is appropriate for a specified agent or context, whether the agent is legitimately authorized to access or use it, and whether it is endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. These dimensions are distinguished from truth, provenance, and technical accessibility: endorsement does not establish truth, and technical retrievability does not establish legitimate access. The framework follows a conservative principle: a qualification must not be assumed merely because a claim exists or can be derived. Missing qualification information is treated as undetermined rather than as an implicit positive or negative judgment. The same principle applies to derived knowledge: an inferred claim cannot automatically inherit the EPB qualifications of its source facts but requires dimension-specific propagation and reassessment. The passport concept is also extended beyond RDF triples to semantic claims produced and manipulated by LLM-based systems, distinguishing computational units such as tokens and semantic spans from epistemic units such as claims and reasoning episodes. The paper develops and analyzes this conceptual and architectural framework, examining its implications for KGs, LLMs, LLM–KG hybrid architectures, and autonomous agents. Rather than reporting an implementation or empirical evaluation, it establishes a basis for explicit, context-sensitive governance of knowledge claims and identifies requirements for their formalization, propagation, and practical assessment.
items.title: Facts Need Passports: Governing Ethics, Privacy, and Bias in Knowledge Graphs

items.summary: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.
items.title: Stochastic Pruning of the DPO Computation Graph: 1.4x Faster Training and Lower Peak Memory

items.summary: Satellite-cloud gaps corrupt the reflectance time series on which computer-agriculture crop-yield estimators depend, and the resulting coverage error propagates into famine early-warning reliability. The framework is evaluated through a replication-based benchmark in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2) and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The benchmark produced an estimated bias of -0.07173 for the intercept and 0.00147 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE values of 0.89562 and 0.0157 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. The coverage-error bound formalises the conditions under which CDA-supported estimators preserve nominal coverage and therefore early-warning reliability, and it identifies the augmentation regimes in which coverage degrades. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and a bound that make the reliability consequences of cloud-gap augmentation auditable rather than assumed.
tags: counterfactual data augmentation; crop-yield estimation; satellite-cloud gaps; coverage-error bound;
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Computer Agriculture Crop-Yield Estimators Under Satellite-Cloud Gaps: An Artificial Intelligence Coverage-Error Bound for Famine Early-Warning Reliability

items.summary: In this work, we assess the recently introduced spin-adapted TDA for spin-flip-down excitations (XSF-TDA) [Mol. Phys. e2631735 (2026)] as a practical approach to this problem. Starting from a high-spin restricted open-shell Kohn--Sham reference, XSF-TDA generates spin-adapted low-spin roots arising from open--open (OO), core--open (CO), open--virtual (OV), and core--virtual (CV) types of spin-flip-down excitations. Across four application sets comprising 243 benchmark cases, XSF-TDA substantially reduces the systematic positive bias observed for TDA and unrestricted spin-flip TDA (USF-TDA). With the B3LYP functional, XSF-TDA reduces the equal-set-weighted macro-MAE relative to USF-TDA from 0.252 eV (0.158 eV) to 0.102~eV (0.056~eV) with the ALDA0 (multicollinear) kernel. Its accuracy is competitive with state-specific $Δ$DFT and quasiparticle-energy DFT (QE-DFT), while being able to provide deeper mechanistic insight through the response vector. In particular, spin-adapted CV configurations provide selected higher-excitation character that strengthens the OO--CV dynamical-spin-polarization channel, which preferentially stabilizes the singlet states. We also identify an INVEST emitter with appreciable OO--OV mixing, suggesting a possible additional contribution to singlet stabilization when the CV contribution is small. The XSF-TDA method therefore provides practical singlet--triplet gap predictions together with interpretable state analysis for the screening and mechanistic understanding of MR-TADF and INVEST emitters.
items.title: Spin-Adapted Spin-Flip Tamm-Dancoff Approximation (XSF-TDA) for Singlet-Triplet Gaps in MR-TADF and INVEST Emitters

items.summary: The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™: Twenty-First Edition Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23547322 15 September 2026 | Revised 21 October 2026 Abstract Bias in artificial intelligence is not a technical accident. It emerges from choices about what knowledge is collected, whose language is centered, which categories are treated as universal, how populations are represented, what objectives models are trained to optimize, and who holds authority over the systems that result. The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™ is an operational decolonial architecture for identifying, interrupting, and replacing the epistemological and governance conditions through which Racial Empire Logic is reproduced in artificial intelligence. Rather than treating bias as a defect that can be corrected solely through post hoc fairness metrics, the Framework moves the site of intervention upstream into data formation, classification, model development, evaluation, deployment, and governance. Xam-Xam bu Gore: The Framework of Liberated Knowledge is the epistemological root of the DIA Framework. Authored by Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz and rooted in Wolof, Afro-Indigenous, and decolonial lineage, Xam-Xam bu Gore establishes that knowledge must exist in a state of liberation from colonial capture, epistemicide, institutional gatekeeping, extraction, and imposed hierarchies of intelligence. Its commitments to epistemological sovereignty, relational knowledge production, living knowledge, and liberation as the governing standard shape the Framework’s treatment of artificial intelligence as a knowledge system rather than a neutral technical instrument. The DIA Framework operationalizes these commitments through Four Pillars: Decolonizing Data Collection, Algorithmic Transparency and Accountability, Intersectional Impact Assessment, and Decolonial AI Governance and Accountability Mechanisms. Together, these pillars locate technical decisions inside their political, historical, cultural, and material conditions. The Framework requires attention to intersecting structures of race, gender, sexuality, disability, neurotype, class, caste, citizenship, language, migration, and colonial status, while rejecting the assumption that Western institutional categories constitute the universal baseline against which all other epistemologies must be measured. This Twenty-First Edition extends the Framework from governance-at-inference toward governance-at-formation through Decolonizing Large-Scale Self-Supervised Pretraining on Heterogeneous Corpora . The protocol identifies corpus construction, provenance, language representation, weighting, training objectives, and corpus revision as sites of epistemic governance. It advances accountable reclamation rather than archival purity, recognizing that knowledge survives through occupation, displacement, translation, institutional capture, resistance, and recovery. Its pluriversal approach seeks meaningful engagement across knowledge systems without requiring those systems to surrender their distinct epistemological structures to a dominant Western frame. Global participation is therefore positioned as decision-making authority over how knowledge enters, shapes, evaluates, and may be revised within an AI system. The edition also provides a corrected mathematical foundation for examining categorical incompleteness and intersectional disparity. Its formal results are deliberately bounded. They show, under stated assumptions, how aggregate parity across coarse categories can conceal disparities among finer community-defined groups and why any fixed category system may require continued refinement and governance. The mathematics does not establish universal elimination of bias, clinical validity, legal validity, ontological completeness, or the effectiveness of any specific deployment. Mathematical guarantees apply only to the quantities, populations, partitions, assump
items.title: The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™: Twenty-First Edition Official Version

items.summary: Nanoscale nonreciprocal elements are needed to control signal flow in scalable quantum technologies, but existing nonreciprocal components are often bulky. Here, we show that a strongly nonreciprocal current-voltage relation can arise entirely from coherent elastic scattering in a mesoscopic Rashba nanowire with gate-defined scatterers. We first identify the symmetry constraints that enforce reciprocal transmission in a phase coherent conductor even when inversion and time-reversal symmetry are broken. We then show how gates that are capacitively coupled to the leads, together with a magnetic scatterer or transverse subband mixing, can remove these constraints. In the weak-scattering regime, nonreciprocal conductance originates from interference between distinct backscattering paths. In the strong-scattering regime, nonreciprocity can be resonantly enhanced by the hybridization of the transmitting channel with bound states that arise from a higher transverse subband or spin-split band. In this regime, we find that a bias-induced change in the gate potentials of about one percent can produce an order-unity diode response, i.e., electrons are transmitted almost as in a clean wire for one bias polarity, whereas for the other polarity the current is strongly suppressed.
items.title: Quantum Interference Enhanced Rectification in Mesoscopic Nanowires
